extracted.intended_audience: public company corporate counsel, compliance officers, and SEC reporting teams
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on when Form 8-K reporting is required for a variety of items (cybersecurity incidents, acquisitions/dispositions, earnings releases, financings, triggering events, exit/disposal activities, impairments, delisting notices) and what disclosures/exhibits and practical steps are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality analysis for cybersecurity incidents (Item 1.05)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a cybersecurity incident is “material” is analyzed under the traditional securities law definition of materiality: an incident is material if “there is a substantial likelihood that a reasonable shareholder would consider it important” in making an investment decision, or if it would have “significantly altered the ‘total mix’ of information made available.” Registrants must consider both qualitative and quantitative factors when assessing materiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies may generally want to consider the following factors when evaluating materiality. Considerations that will not be relevant: (1) Whether the affected system was owned or operated by the registrant or a third-party; (2) Inability to determine the full extent of the incident; (3) Ongoing nature of the registrant’s internal investigation; (4) Timing of sharing information about the incident with governmental authorities or others. Quantitative considerations: reasonably expected percentage impact on revenue due to lost sales; percentage impact on net income due to lost revenues, containment/remediation expenses (including ransom) and other expected expenses (regulatory/legal proceedings, voluntary mitigation); percentage impact on total and current assets from expenses associated with the incident. Qualitative considerations: relative importance of systems affected (including expected downtime); duration of incident, detection method, readiness of response; ability to restore systems and expected integrity; nature and scope/magnitude of information accessed or exfiltrated; effect on “crown jewels”; harm to reputation/brand; impact on supply chain and operations; impact on relationships with customers, suppliers, partners; effect on competitive position; likelihood of regulatory actions; likelihood of private litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 2.01 — Completion of acquisition or disposition of assets: when an 8-K is required
rubrics_metrics.description: An 8-K is required if the company or any of its consolidated subsidiaries has completed the acquisition or disposition of a significant amount of assets, otherwise than in the ordinary course of business, or a significant amount of assets that constitute a real estate operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions/explanations: “Acquisition” includes purchase, acquisition by lease, exchange, merger, consolidation, succession or other acquisition (but not construction or acquisition of materials for construction). “Disposition” includes sale, disposition by lease, exchange, merger, consolidation, mortgage, assignment, hypothecation, abandonment, destruction, or other disposition; an indefinite closing of part of facilities with a write-down >10% constitutes an “other disposition.” Instruction 4: an acquisition/disposition is “significant” if (i) equity in net book value or amount paid/received exceeds 10% of total assets of the company and consolidated subsidiaries, or (ii) it involved a “business” that is “significant” as defined in Rule 11-01 of Regulation S-X. When an acquisition/disposition involves a “business,” apply the 20% significance tests (clause (ii)) and not the 10% tests (clause (i)). The acquisition of a “business” includes interests accounted for under the equity method or fair value option. Timing: an Item 2.01 8-K is required only when the acquisition or disposition is consummated (execution of agreement may be reportable under Item 1.01). Required disclosure: date of completion; brief description of assets; identity of counterparty and nature of any material relationship; nature and amount of consideration and, if a material relationship exists, formula/principle for determining amount; exhibits required: financial statements of businesses acquired (Item 9.01), pro forma financial information (Item 9.01), and copies of plans of acquisition or disposition. Practice tips: e.g., aggregate impact of acquired businesses not required unless related and significant in the aggregate; minority cost-method purchases that do not result in control generally do not require filing financials; be mindful when filing acquiree historical and pro forma statements in registration statements; subsidiaries acquiring from a parent may trigger filing by the subsidiary not the parent; SEC staff positions about consolidated subsidiaries and age of financial statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 2.02 — Results of operations and financial condition: triggers and exemptions
rubrics_metrics.description: An 8-K is required if the company, or any person acting on its behalf, makes any public announcement or release disclosing material non-public information regarding the company’s results of operations or financial condition for a completed quarterly or annual fiscal period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditional exemption for oral/telephonic/webcast/broadcast disclosure: a Form 8-K is not required if (a) the information is provided as part of a presentation complementary to, and initially occurs within 48 hours after, a related written announcement or release that has been furnished on Form 8-K; (b) the presentation is broadly accessible to the public; (c) the financial and other statistical information is provided on the company’s website together with any information required under Regulation G; and (d) the presentation was announced by a widely disseminated press release including instructions on accessing the presentation and location on the company website. Required disclosure: brief identification of the announcement or release; text of that announcement or release as an exhibit to the Form 8-K.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-GAAP financial measure requirements when furnishing Item 2.02 disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Form 8-K furnished under Item 2.02 includes any non-GAAP financial measures, the company must comply with Regulation G and certain requirements of Item 10(e) of Regulation S-K.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Regulation G: accompany non-GAAP measure with the most directly comparable GAAP measure; provide a reconciliation (quantitative for historic measures; qualitative may suffice for forward-looking if quantitative reconciliation would be unreasonable); include other information necessary to prevent the non-GAAP measure from being misleading. Item 10(e)(1)(i) requires: presentation with equal or greater prominence of the most directly comparable GAAP measure; same reconciliation as Regulation G; explanation of why management believes the non-GAAP measure is useful to investors; and, to the extent material, disclosure of other purposes management uses the non-GAAP measures for. SEC staff has focused on compliance with the equal or greater prominence requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and scope considerations for Item 2.02 (pre-announcements, 48-hour safe harbor, oral disclosures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Item 2.02 is only triggered by public disclosure of material non-public information regarding a completed fiscal period; earnings guidance for periods not ended does not by itself trigger the item. The 48-hour safe harbor is literal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If guidance for a period not ended is included in an announcement regarding a completed period (e.g., Q2 guidance included in Q1 results), the guidance is part of the document that must be furnished. Earnings pre-announcements or warnings prior to the end of the quarter do not trigger the item, but pre-announcements after quarter-end do (preliminary earnings release after quarter-end, even if estimates, will trigger Item 2.02). The 48-hour safe harbor is construed literally and is not equivalent to two business or calendar days. Be careful about language used to refer to exhibits so as not to change their status from furnished to filed. When preparing registration statements that incorporate by reference prior Exchange Act filings, avoid unintentionally incorporating Form 8-Ks that were furnished under Item 2.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 2.03 — Creation of a direct financial obligation or obligation under an off-balance sheet arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: An 8-K is required if the company becomes obligated on a direct financial obligation that is material to the company, or becomes directly or contingently liable for a material obligation arising out of an off-balance sheet arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions: “Direct financial obligation” includes (1) a long-term debt obligation; (2) a finance lease obligation; (3) an operating lease obligation; or (4) a short-term debt obligation arising other than in the ordinary course of business. Off-balance sheet arrangement includes transactions where the registrant has: (1) any obligation under a guarantee contract with characteristics identified in ASC 460-10-15-4; (2) a retained or contingent interest in assets transferred to an unconsolidated entity that serves as credit/liquidity/market risk support; (3) any obligation that would be accounted for as a derivative instrument except when indexed to the registrant's own stock and classified in equity per ASC 815; or (4) any obligation arising out of a variable interest in an unconsolidated entity that is material and provides financing, liquidity, market risk or credit risk support, or engages in leasing, hedging or R&D services. Required disclosure: date company becomes obligated; brief description of transaction/agreement; for direct financial obligations: amount, terms of payment, brief description of material acceleration/increase terms, nature of any recourse provisions; for off-balance sheet arrangements: description of nature and amount of obligation, material terms under which it may become direct or be accelerated, nature of recourse provisions, maximum potential future payments (undiscounted), and brief description of other material terms/conditions. Practice tips: filing obligation arises when agreement enforceable against company; if arrangement creates potential obligations across multiple transactions, file upon entering facility/program and monitor aggregate takedowns; establish quantitative guideposts for what constitutes material debt but remember materiality is facts-and-circumstances qualitative determination; certain securities sold under effective registration statements may be exempt; disclosure required about off-balance sheet arrangements even if company is not a party to the underlying agreement; subsidiaries' obligations may trigger the item if material; consider reporting under Item 3.03 if credit agreements include dividend-limiting covenants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 2.04 — Triggering events that accelerate or increase obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: An 8-K is required if a “triggering event” (e.g., event of default, event of acceleration) causing the increase or acceleration of a direct financial obligation occurs and the consequences are material, or if a triggering event increases or accelerates the company's obligation under an off-balance sheet arrangement or causes a contingent obligation to become a direct financial obligation and the consequences are material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions: direct financial obligation and off-balance sheet arrangement have the same meanings as under Item 2.03; direct financial obligation also includes obligations arising out of off-balance sheet arrangements that are accrued under ASC 450-20-25 as a probable loss contingency. Required disclosure: date of triggering event; brief description of the underlying agreement/transaction/arrangement; brief description of the triggering event; amount of direct financial obligation or amount and nature of off-balance sheet obligation as increased, if applicable; terms of payment or acceleration that apply; any other material obligation that may arise, increase, be accelerated or become direct as a result of the triggering event. Practice tips: in assessing materiality consider cross-default or cross-acceleration provisions; no disclosure required unless and until triggering event has occurred (including satisfaction of conditions), except passage of time alone; if agreement requires notice to company for event to occur, no disclosure required until notice given; a notice of default is a triggering event even if matter is pending with an arbitrator; voluntary redemption of convertible notes by company is not a triggering event; inventory agreements and aggregate monitoring recommended; triggering events by subsidiaries may trigger this item if material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 2.05 — Costs associated with exit or disposal activities: triggers and disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: An 8-K is required within four business days after the company’s board, a board committee, or an authorized officer commits the company to an exit or disposal plan, disposes of a long-lived asset, or terminates employees under a plan of termination, if material charges will be incurred under GAAP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required disclosure: date of commitment to course of action; description of course of action including facts and circumstances leading to expected action; expected completion date; estimate of total amount or range expected to be incurred (aggregate and for each major type of cost); estimate of amount or range that will result in future cash expenditures. If a required estimate cannot be made at initial filing, company must amend the Form 8-K within four business days after it formulates the estimate. Practice tips: item captures write-offs and restructurings; company is not obligated to disclose an estimate in the initial Form 8-K if unable to make a good faith estimate but should provide one when possible; inability to estimate could trigger adverse investor reaction so may wish to postpone commitment until estimate available; consider implementing procedures to make clear when a commitment has been made; “commitment” means reaching a final determination regarding a course of action; costs reportable are not limited to ASC 420 costs; disclosure of terminations as part of a plan may be required even if underlying business not substantially altered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 2.06 — Material impairments: triggers, required disclosure, and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: An 8-K is required if the company's board, a board committee, or an authorized officer concludes that a material charge for impairment to one or more of the company's assets is required under GAAP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required disclosure: date of conclusion that a material charge is required; description of impaired assets; facts and circumstances leading to conclusion; estimate of amount or range of impairment charge; estimate of amount or range that will result in future cash expenditures. If a required estimate cannot be made at initial filing, the Form 8-K must be amended within four business days after the company makes such estimate. Practice tips: terminology is based on ASC 360-10; reportable impairments include impairments of securities or goodwill; no 8-K required if impairment conclusion is made in connection with preparation/review/audit of financial statements required in next periodic report, the report is timely filed, and the impairment conclusion is disclosed in that report; procedures should make clear when a conclusion has been reached as opposed to active consideration; consider applicability of Item 2.01 when impaired assets are significant; the SEC staff has indicated that re-measurement of a deferred tax asset due to change in tax rule/law is not an impairment under ASC 740.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 3.01 — Notice of delisting or failure to satisfy continued listing rule or standard; transfer of listing
rubrics_metrics.description: An 8-K is required if the company receives notice from the national securities exchange that the company or its securities do not satisfy a continued listing rule or standard, the exchange has applied to the SEC to delist such securities, the exchange has taken necessary steps to delist, the company notifies the exchange it is aware of material noncompliance, the exchange issues a public reprimand, or the company's board has taken action to withdraw listing or transfer listing to another exchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required disclosure (partial in this excerpt): date of notice or action; rule or standard in question that the company fails, or has failed, to satisfy. (Document continues with further required disclosure items and practice considerations not included in this chunk.)
